blocks.text: The reason for these prohibitions seems to have been wholly mystical. 1. God forbade the birds of prey, namely the eagle, the ossifrage, the kite, the vulture, the hawk, the raven, etc., in order to turn the Jews away from robbery. 2. The nocturnal birds, namely the eagle owl, the little owl and the bat, so that they might cast off the works of darkness and show themselves children of light. 3. The birds of lakes and riverbanks, such as the onocrotalus, the catarrhactes, the pelican and the stork, [III, 123] whose food is most impure, and the hoopoe, which nests in dung, so as to keep them from all uncleanness. 4. Finally the ostrich, which does not rise from the ground, so that, leaving earthly things behind, they might strive toward the things that are above. This explanation is not ours but that of the ancient interpreters. Aristeas: Περὶ ὧν δὲ ἀπηγόρευται πτηνῶν, εὑρήσεις ἄγριά τε, καὶ σαρκοφάγα, καὶ καταδυναστεύοντα τῇ περὶ ταῦτα δυνάμει τὰ λοιπά· [Peri hōn de apēgoreutai ptēnōn, heurēseis agria te, kai sarkophaga, kai katadynasteuonta tē peri tauta dynamei ta loipa] As for the birds that are forbidden, you will find that they are wild and carnivorous, and by their strength exercise tyranny over the others. Barnabas at once transfers this to morals in the Epistle which our eminent Vossius edited: Οὐδὲ μὴ φάγῃς, φησὶ, τὸν ἀετὸν, οὐδὲ τὸν ὀξύπτερον, οὐδὲ τὸν ἰκτῖνα, οὐδὲ τὸν κόρακα· οὐ μὴ, φησὶ, κολληθήσῃ ἀνθρώποις τοιούτοις, οἵ τινες οὐκ οἴδασι διὰ κόπου καὶ ἱδρῶτος πορίζειν ἑαυτοῖς τὴν τροφὴν, ἀλλ' ἁρπάζουσι τὰ ἀλλότρια ἐν ἀνομίᾳ αὐτῶν· [Oude mē phagēs, phēsi, ton aeton, oude ton oxypteron, oude ton iktina, oude ton koraka; ou mē, phēsi, kollēthēsē anthrōpois toioutois, hoi tines ouk oidasi dia kopou kai hidrōtos porizein heautois tēn trophēn, all' harpazousi ta allotria en anomia autōn] Nor shall you eat, he says, the eagle, or the hawk, or the raven: that is, you shall not join yourself to those who do not know how to earn their living by toil and sweat, but seize what belongs to others through their iniquity. Clement of Alexandria, not content with having quoted this in book 5 of the Stromata, also imitates it thus in the Paedagogus, book 3, chapter 11: Οὐδ' ἰκτῖνα, ἢ ὠκύπτερον μαστοφαγῆ, ἢ [col. 356] ἀετὸν φάγῃς, φησίν· οὐκ ἐγγιεῖς, φησὶν, τοῖς δι' ἁπαγῆς τὸν βίον πορίζομένοις· [Oud' iktina, ē ōkypteron mastophagē, ē aeton phagēs, phēsin; ouk engieis, phēsin, tois di' hapagēs ton bion porizomenois] You shall not eat the kite, or the hawk that devours breasts, or the eagle: that is, do not approach those who obtain their living by plunder. Origen, in Homily 7 on Leviticus, says: You shall not eat these, because they are unclean: the eagle, and the vulture, and the rest like them. For these birds always feed on dead bodies, and live off dead carcasses. All, therefore, who lead a life of this kind are to be held unclean. I think that those too are named in these who brood over the deaths of others, etc., as if gaping after the carcasses of the dead. In the same place he also asserts that those who in their words display heavenly learning, yet in their deeds perform carnal and dead works, are rightly called vultures and eagles, which swoop down from the heights upon dead and stinking flesh. And a little later: Some love not so much rapacity as obscurity and darkness. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, like little owls and bats, etc. Novatian, On Jewish Foods, chapter 3: Who (would make food of) the raven? But he execrates crafty dispositions. When he forbids the sparrow (he meant στρουθὸν [strouthon], that is, the ostrich), he rebukes intemperance. When the little owl, he hates those who flee the light of truth. When the swan, the proud with lofty neck. When the charadrius, the excessively chattering intemperance of the tongue. When the bat, those who seek the darkness of night and of error alike. In Cyril, book 9 Against Julian, eagles, hawks, catarrhactae, griffins and vultures signify the rapacious and greedy; the raven, the shifty; the hoopoe, little owl and bat, the ignorant and lovers of darkness, who hate the light of doctrine. And in book 14 On Adoration the same author has much more on the same subject. There too he counts not only the hoopoe but also the heron and the charadrius [III, 124] among the nocturnal birds together with the little owl and the bat, asserting that γλαῦκα, καὶ ἐρωδιὸν, καὶ χαραδριὸν, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτοῦ, ἐπόπα, καὶ νυκτερίδα [glauka, kai erōdion, kai charadrion, kai ta homoia autou, epopa, kai nykterida], the little owl, and the heron, and the charadrius, and those like them, the hoopoe and the bat, are rejected as νυκτὸς φίλα, καὶ χαίροντα μὲν τῷ σκότει, καὶ πτήσει ὡς ἡδυτάτην ἐν αὐτῷ ποιεῖσθαι μεμελετηκότα, κατεχθραίνοντα δὲ τὸ ἡλίου φῶς, καὶ τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ τι δρᾷν μὴ ἀνεχόμενα [nyktos phila, kai chaironta men tō skotei, kai ptēsei hōs hēdytatēn en autō poieisthai memeletēkota, katechthrainonta de to hēliou phōs, kai to en autō ti dran mē anechomena], birds that are friends of the night, delight in darkness, and are accustomed to fly more gladly in it, and that shrink from the light of the sun and cannot bear to undertake anything in it. This indeed fits the little owl and the bat, but not the hoopoe, the heron and the charadrius. Yet Procopius of Gaza follows Cyril on this point in his Commentaries on Leviticus. But in matters pertaining to nature the sacred doctors are not always to be trusted, since cares of greater moment did not allow them to devote serious attention to these trifles.
